THE EPISTEMOLOGY OF ACTION: ABHINAVA'S METAPHYSICS OF AGENCY

How the IPVV proves causality is the conscious knower's agency — the kriyādhikāra's argument-chain (V3A–I)

  • 026-08-11. The recognition-thesis is not only an epistemology (knowledge is the felt self-awareness)
  • t a metaphysics of action. In the kriyādhikāra, Abhinavagupta argues that causality itself is the
  • nscious knower's agency — that cause and effect are, in their essence, the relation of agent and
  • ject of action. This essay reconstructs the argument-chain in full: the timeless that manifests order,
  • e bhedābheda action-cognitions, the inert-cannot-cause proof, inference across knowers, and the will
  • cause-agent-action. It is the kriyādhikāra essay, and it is unique to the completed IPVV — this is
  • e region Ratié's book does not develop.*

1. The problem: how can the timeless act?

  • e kriyādhikāra opens the parallel — having established the power of knowledge, now the power of
  • tion. And it confronts the paradox at the heart of the system: the Lord is beyond time and sequence,
  • t the world he manifests is shot through with sequence — causes before effects, moments before moments.
  • e IPVV announces the answer in the opening verse of homage:
"He bows to Śiva, who, though free of sequence, manifests manifold sequences." (V3A)
  • The mirror.** The image is the mirror: a mirror bears countless reflections — of things before it,
  • side it, in all their variety — without ever ceasing to be the one, undivided mirror. It is not torn
  • to pieces by what it shows. So too the one consciousness, whose essence is nothing but appearance, can
  • ke up within itself a host of seemingly contradictory forms without its oneness being divided.
  • The first claim.** This is the "action-support" (kriyāśraya): the one that acts is one, and it is
  • ecisely because it is one and un-divided that it can show sequence at all. The timeless manifests
  • der because its oneness is not threatened by the order.

2. Against the Buddhist: the five refutations (V3A)

  • e IPVV aims this squarely at the Buddhist, who had said: only momentary cognitions flash forth, with
  • owner behind them; memory is nothing but impression; cognition is either inert or without real
  • mporal distinctions. Abhinavagupta answers each point:
  • Distinct cognitions cannot serve the dealings of the world. A string of unrelated flashes could
  • ver get anyone to the village.
  • Memory is not mere impression. Memory is the un-broken manifestation (V2A).
  • Cognition is the un-contracted consciousness, contracting itself by its own power under the tint
  • the known object.
  • Its oneness is not threatened by its many appearances, any more than a mirror's is by its
  • flections.
  • The first objection, rejected.** "The action of the one is not ordered" is rejected by establishing
  • at one as the agent: the one can be of many natures; that is not a contradiction.

3. The action-cognitions as bhedābheda (V3B)

  • e IPVV then takes up the cognitions of action — the bhedābheda (distinction-and-non-distinction)
  • marśa:
"The cognitions of action, relation, universal, substance, direction and time have a substrate that
is at once one and many, and they are to be accepted as true — true by their stability and true by
their efficacy." (V3B)
  • The example.** The body of Caitra — and of Maitra — although it differs according to this or that
  • ace, time, and shape, nevertheless shines forth without ever abandoning its oneness, in the recognition
  • his is the very same body." That very unity is the action, in the judgment "Caitra is walking." The
  • tion-cognitions are both one and many, and they are true by their stability and efficacy.
  • The functionalist criterion.** This is where the IPVV gives the "true by stability and use" — the
  • gnitions of action are accepted as true because they are stable (no refutation uproots them) and
  • ficacious (they serve the intended end). This is the functionalist criterion that deepens the
  • rma-freedom resolution.

4. The inert cannot be a cause (V3G)

  • e hard work of the kriyādhikāra is to show that the inert cannot be a cause. The argument:
  • The seed and the sprout.** The inert seed cannot endow the sprout with being — for the sprout is either
  • ready existent (in which case nothing is acquired) or non-existent (in which case it cannot come to
  • , since the non-existent has no nature by which to gain existence). The claim that the effect is both
  • istent and non-existent, or neither, is self-contradictory. The blue cannot become yellow, however
  • rd we try; so the non-existent cannot acquire existence.
  • The conclusion.** Hence the inert, material cause has no real causal power. The real cause is
  • sewhere — in the conscious:
"The potter creates the pot by his power; the yogin, by his will alone, brings about an effect without
any clay or seed. If the inert seed and clay were the true causes, this would be impossible. But it is
not impossible — which shows that the true cause is consciousness, the free will that shapes the
effect." (V3G)
  • The thesis.** Causality is the conscious knower's agency. The essence of cause and effect is nothing
  • t the relation of agent and object of action.

5. Inference across knowers (V3H)

  • e Vijñānavādin objects: if everything is appearance, cause and effect are only relations between
  • pearances — and the smoke-appearance can never reach the fire-appearance of another stream.
  • The answer (V3H):** the Lord creates the appearances for all the knowers at once, as one.
"So when we grasp the pervasion — that smoke implies fire — the smoke-appearance and the
fire-appearance belong, in the Lord's single creation, to every knower alike... The fire-appearance is
one, not split by the difference of streams; so the smoke can arise from it and from nothing else."
(V3H)
  • The result.** Inference holds across knowers because the Lord has created the appearances as one. The
  • ause of the Lord" (adhipatipratyaya) is the fire-appearance, indirect to the one who infers, by which
  • e inference is made. This grounds shared inference in the one creation.

6. The will as cause, agent, and action (V3I)

  • e crown of the kriyādhikāra is the sharpest objection and its answer.
  • The objection.** If consciousness is one — if all the world is a single consciousness — then how is
  • tion possible? Action needs an agent and an object, two distinct things; but if all is one, there is
  • distinct object for the agent to act upon.
  • The answer.** Action is the one will-to-do that joins the agent and the object:
"There is a single re-recollection (parāmarśa) marked by the will-to-do — the moment 'I will make
this' — which rests, as it were, in the other consciousness-essence and binds the two together. It is
this one will-recollection, and not any external contact, that makes the jar an object of action and
consciousness its agent." (V3I)
  • And the refutation of the monist's "ignorance."** Against the Advaita's claim that the difference is
  • re ignorance, the IPVV asks: of whom is this ignorance? The one-form Brahman cannot have it; the
  • parate souls would be raised up by it; "un-explainable" is the speech of a yakṣa. The difference is
  • al:
"Our cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference, and the very 'refutation'
that would remove difference is itself a manifestation — and so would be difference, and so would be
ignorance." (V3I)
  • The summit (the will as the three):**
"The cause does not cause, the agent does not act, the action does not move — all three are the one
will, by which the Lord, wishing to stand, becomes the world." (V3I)

7. The complete argument-chain

  • e kriyādhikāra's argument, completely stated:
  • The timeless manifests order (V3A) — because the one is one, it can show sequence without
  • vision (the mirror).
  • The action-cognitions are bhedābheda (V3B) — one and many, true by stability and efficacy.
  • The inert cannot cause (V3G) — the seed cannot endow the sprout (the existent/non-existent
  • lemma); the real cause is the conscious, the free will.
  • Inference holds across knowers (V3H) — because the Lord creates the appearances as one.
  • The will is cause, agent, and action (V3I) — the one will-to-do joins agent and object; the
  • fference is real, not ignorance.
  • The conclusion.** Causality is the conscious knower's agency. Action is not an external event; it is
  • e will of consciousness. The one who knows is the one who acts; knowledge and action are the two faces
  • the one self-awareness. This is the epistemology of action — the region that completes the
  • cognition-thesis as a metaphysics.

8. The significance for the recognition-thesis

  • e kriyādhikāra matters for recognition because it completes the parallel:
  • The jñānādhikāra established: knowledge is the felt self-awareness.
  • The kriyādhikāra establishes: action is the same self-awareness, as the will.
  • e recognition-thesis is not only "knowledge is self-aware"; it is "the self-aware consciousness is
  • so the agent." And recognition — the re-cognition of the self as the Lord — re-cognizes the self as
  • e doer as well as the knower. The Lord is the one who knows and acts (the jñāna-kriyā pair). The
  • iyādhikāra gives the action-side of the recognition: the same felt self-awareness, in its freedom, is
  • e agent of the world.

9. The boundary

  • e kriyādhikāra's arguments are [T] and largely sound: the inert-cannot-cause, the bhedābheda
  • tion-cognitions, the will-as-the-three are argued. The one commitment is the same as everywhere: the
  • ep from "each field's action is its own will" to "all action is one will" (the universalization). The
  • ert-cannot-cause proves the conscious agent per field; the identity of all agents is the commitment.
  • e epistemology of action is argued for the finite field; the one agent is the wager.
  • his is the epistemology-of-action essay. The kriyādhikāra argues that causality is the conscious
  • ower's agency: the timeless manifests order (V3A), the action-cognitions are bhedābheda (V3B), the
  • ert cannot cause (V3G), inference holds across knowers by the one creation (V3H), and the will is
  • use-agent-action (V3I). This completes the recognition-thesis: the self-aware consciousness is also
  • e agent. The one commitment is the universalization (one agent). This is the region Ratié's book does
  • t develop.*
